name: Webflow development
summary: Sites your team can actually edit. Planned, designed in Figma and built in Webflow from the ground up, with clean classes, a CMS that makes sense and motion that survives a copy edit.
solve-1-problem: Every text change needs a developer.
solve-1-answer: Content lives in the CMS and sections are built to be reused, so updates take minutes, not tickets.
solve-2-problem: The site looks like every other template.
solve-2-answer: Each page is designed around what you do, then built from scratch instead of bent from a theme.
solve-3-problem: Animations break the moment copy changes.
solve-3-answer: Interactions hook onto stable classes and CMS fields, so new content animates the same way.
deliverable-1-desc: Structure agreed before a pixel moves.
deliverable-2-desc: Every page and state, desktop to phone.
deliverable-4-desc: Collections shaped around how you publish.
deliverable-6-desc: An editing guide plus a walkthrough video.
stage-1-desc: A call about goals, audience and what the site has to do.
stage-2-desc: Sitemap, wireframes, then the full design in Figma.
stage-3-desc: Webflow from the ground up: components, CMS, motion.
stage-4-desc: QA, a Lighthouse pass, launch day and a walkthrough.
code: Built to be edited

name: WebGL + data
summary: Three.js globes and D3 maps embedded in Webflow and fed by the CMS. Your data becomes something visitors can spin, zoom and explore.
best-for: Studios, firms and brands with reach
solve-1-problem: Your reach is a paragraph nobody reads.
solve-1-answer: Projects pin themselves to a live globe from the CMS, so a new project is a new pin.
solve-2-answer: Case results plot onto an interactive map, state by state, straight from your content.
solve-3-problem: 3D usually means a slow, fragile site.
solve-3-answer: The heavy pieces load on scroll, pause off-screen and fall back gracefully on older phones.
deliverable-1-desc: The CMS fields your globe or map reads from.
deliverable-2-desc: Three.js or D3, embedded cleanly in Webflow.
deliverable-3-desc: Add an item, the visual updates itself.
deliverable-4-desc: Cards, tooltips and deep links per point.
deliverable-6-desc: Hosted on GitHub with a changelog.
stage-1-desc: What you have, where it lives, what it should show.
stage-2-desc: A rough, working globe or map to react to early.
stage-3-desc: Styled, interactive and reading from your CMS.
stage-4-desc: Performance, mobile gestures and edge cases.

name: Motion + interaction
summary: Scroll systems, drag physics and micro-interactions with easing tuned by hand. Motion that explains, rewards and makes a site feel alive, without getting in the way.
solve-1-problem: The site is static and forgettable.
solve-1-answer: A signature interaction gives visitors a reason to stay, play and share the link.
solve-2-answer: Every curve is chosen for what it communicates, not dragged from a preset.
solve-3-problem: Motion makes some visitors feel sick.
solve-3-answer: Every effect has a reduced-motion version, so the site works for everyone.
deliverable-1-desc: What moves, why, and how it feels.
deliverable-2-desc: Key interactions to try before the build.
stage-1-desc: Find the two or three places motion earns its keep.
stage-2-desc: Build them rough and try them on real devices.
stage-3-desc: Tune timing and easing until it feels right.
stage-4-desc: Reduced motion, performance and mobile checks.

name: Logo + brand identity
summary: Logos, color, type and brand rules built on a grid, so they hold up from a favicon to a billboard, and give your website something real to stand on.
solve-1-problem: The logo falls apart at small sizes.
solve-1-answer: A constructed mark with clear proportions that stays sharp from 16 pixels up.
solve-2-problem: Every new asset looks a bit different.
solve-2-answer: Color, type and spacing rules your team can follow without a designer in the room.
solve-3-problem: The brand does not say what you stand for.
solve-3-answer: Strategy first: the identity grows out of who you are and who you serve.
deliverable-1-desc: Values, audience and personality, written down.
deliverable-3-desc: Palettes and pairings with usage rules.
stage-1-desc: Who you are, who you serve and what you want to feel like.
stage-2-desc: Two or three distinct concepts to react to.
stage-3-desc: One direction, sharpened on the grid.
stage-4-desc: Guidelines, assets and files, ready to use.

name: Custom deploys
summary: Coded sites in Astro or Next.js, deployed on Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare, for the projects where Webflow is not the right fit. Same care, different engine.
solve-1-problem: Webflow cannot do what you need.
solve-1-answer: When logins, big datasets or custom logic outgrow Webflow, a coded build takes over.
solve-2-problem: Developers hand over a black box.
solve-2-answer: Typed, documented and versioned, so the next developer can pick it up.
solve-3-answer: Previews for every change and one-click rollbacks when something goes wrong.
deliverable-1-desc: Why this stack, and what it costs to run.
deliverable-2-desc: The same design process as every build.
deliverable-3-desc: Astro or Next.js, components and content.
deliverable-6-desc: A README a human can follow.
stage-1-desc: Make sure a coded build is actually the right call.
stage-2-desc: Figma first, same as any mission.
stage-4-desc: Deploy pipeline, monitoring and a handoff.

name: Advanced CMS integrations
summary: Airtable, Google Sheets or any API piped into the Webflow CMS, with filters, multi-references and pages that build themselves. The connected content system behind the site.
solve-1-answer: Update the sheet or database you already use, and the site follows.
solve-2-problem: Related content is linked by hand.
solve-2-answer: Multi-references tie projects, services and people together, so every page points somewhere useful.
solve-3-answer: Filter, sort and search across collections without a page reload.
deliverable-2-desc: Airtable, Sheets or API into the CMS.
deliverable-6-desc: How to add, edit and publish.
stage-1-desc: What exists, where it lives and how it connects.
stage-2-desc: Collections, fields and references in Webflow.
stage-3-desc: Sync the source and wire the templates.
stage-4-desc: Edge cases, limits and editor training.
code-label: Sync · sheet row to CMS item

name: Design systems
summary: Variables, components and type scales that keep page ten as sharp as page one, in Figma and in Webflow, named the same in both.
solve-1-problem: Every new page drifts a little further.
solve-1-answer: Shared tokens and components make the right choice the easy one.
solve-2-problem: Design and build use different names.
solve-2-answer: The same variable names in Figma and Webflow, so handoffs stop losing things.
solve-3-answer: Update a token and it ripples through every page.
deliverable-2-desc: Fluid sizes that work on every screen.
deliverable-4-desc: The same tokens, live in the build.
deliverable-5-desc: When and how to use each piece.
stage-1-desc: Collect what exists and where it drifts.
stage-2-desc: Define the foundations everything builds on.
stage-3-desc: Build the pieces in Figma and Webflow.
stage-4-desc: Rules and examples your team can follow.

name: Performance
summary: Lazy-loaded WebGL, reduced-motion fallbacks and a Lighthouse pass on every page. Ambitious visuals that still load fast on a phone on the train.
solve-1-problem: The site is beautiful and slow.
solve-1-answer: Heavy pieces wait until they are needed, so the first screen loads right away.
solve-2-problem: Phones heat up and scrolling stutters.
solve-2-answer: Animations run on the GPU, pause off-screen and scale down on lower-power phones.
solve-3-problem: Nobody knows why the score dropped.
solve-3-answer: Every page gets a Lighthouse pass and a short report of what changed and why.
deliverable-3-desc: WebGL and embeds load on demand.
deliverable-4-desc: Duplicate libraries and dead code removed.
deliverable-6-desc: Before and after, in plain language.
stage-2-desc: Fix what visitors actually feel first.
stage-4-desc: Measure again and write it up.
